title: From toddlers to babies
caption: The galaxy cluster RXC J0032.1+1808, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Galaxies glow against the dark like fireflies or floating embers from a bonfire. Together they form RXC J0032.1+1808, a massive cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity, photographed by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3.

The image comes from RELICS, the Reionization Lensing Cluster Survey, which imaged 41 massive galaxy clusters. Its goal was to find the brightest distant galaxies for the James Webb Space Telescope to follow up.

Webb was built to see in infrared, which matters for the most distant objects. Because the Universe is expanding, light from very distant galaxies is strongly redshifted, stretched towards the red end of the spectrum and beyond, so infrared telescopes are needed to study them. The source compares the galaxies Hubble can reach, billions of years back in time, to toddlers. Webb was designed to reach the babies, the very first galaxies that formed in the Universe.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed the cluster in visible and near-infrared light, from 435 nm to 1.6 μm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Much of this light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the distant galaxies are far too faint to see without Hubble.

explore: When this picture was released, the source expected Webb to launch in 2018. The cluster images from RELICS were meant to give the new telescope a ready list of bright, distant galaxies worth studying in detail.
alt: Many glowing galaxies scattered across a dark background.
